Raspberry Pi is unleashing a storm of creative computing
I've been meaning to buy one of these

The Zero I have is kinda fun to play around with but unless you've got a very specific purpose to buy one for then the Zero isn't worth it because it will cost you a lot more than $5 to turn into a usable micro computer and the Zero isn't alone in this regard, most of these kinds of devices have the same "bare bones is almost useless" problem.

When you factor in the cost of a usb hub (very cheap ebay hubs might not work), a usb wifi adaptor (in a pinch a decent android phone with tethering can work), a keyboard + mouse, a micro hdmi to normal hdmi adapter, and most importantly a micro SD memory card the price can go up quite a bit. If you've got all this stuff just lying around then go for it, you won't regret it but don't get suckered in with the idea its a fully functional $5 computer.

Consequently, I have been waiting for them to be in stock to grab one. I have a regular Pi and I have not really been satisfied with it. It's too slow to use as a usable computer and too big and expensive to be embedded.
Zero isn't much better than Rasberry PI B+ because the it has to be overclocked to hit that advertized 1ghz clock speed. Pi 2 would be a lot quicker with its quad core cpu.
The point is that it isn't usable as a general purpose computer. At least the Zero is embeddable so there's that.

Its not really, no charging circuitry for battery operation, no internal storage, you have to add accessories (wifi, bluetooth, keyboard+mouse etc) if you want to do anything with it and if you've got the know how it can be configured for headless operation but really its just intended to be an extremely affordable and basic computer, a 10-20 dollar computer to get you started messing with a computer maybe get you started doing some programming or cutting your teeth on linux.

no charging circuitry for battery operation,

Neither do most microcontrollers. Charging circuitry can easily be implemented outboard.

no internal storage

That;s true and annoying

wifi, bluetooth, keyboard+mouse etc)

Maybe your idea of "embedded" is different than mine. Certainly no need for bluetooth and probably not wifi. For interface, a touch screen could be used -- or navigation menus with buttons on the GPIOs

its just intended to be an extremely affordable and basic computer,

Which the Pi fails miserably at IMO

But if you do go through the trouble of configuring it to use an alternate display system, it could be a decent embedded board for a decent price. Linux has a fair amount of drivers for displays connected through serial, parallel, SPI, I2C etc

My idea of embedded is something that can easily take inputs and produce outputs be it a button or sensor as an input and either storing that input or simply flashing an LED as an output but for your average Joe McNobody that means some kind of a human interface e.g. keyboard input and video output because there is no direct way to interface and program the Pi to function that way without going though Raspbian or something similar, a touch screen display isn't that cheap and isn't plug and play like a TV would be (I'll eat those words if it is stupid easy when I get myself a nice touch screen for my Pi).

All you need to make a very simple computer is a human readable output and an input and the Pi does it well enough that you can use it for basic stuff like light media consumption or a little bit of programming. If I remember right the whole thing is meant to be an educational product anyway. Pi's are odd things, they occupy a space that is not quite a microcontroller and not quite a normal computer but can be a bit of both at the same time but at all times it leans heavily towards being a cheap and basic light usage computer.

Just a bit more on alt displays I dug out an old 5510 screen I had for arduino projects, should be a bit of fun.
